analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to force recalls of unsafe food, drugs, and cosmetics and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after a single committee hearing in May 1992, it died in the Senate committee when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have strengthened the FDA's hand against unsafe products. It would have let courts and the Health and Human Services Secretary order companies to stop distributing and recall food, drugs, or cosmetics that could cause serious harm or death. It also would have let the FDA issue subpoenas, inspect factories and records more broadly, tighten screening of imported goods, and fine companies up to $3 million for violations, false statements, or bribing inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices — essentially everyone. The bill's mandatory stop-distribution and recall orders would remove dangerous products from shelves faster than the current voluntary system, and civil penalties would give companies a financial reason to fix problems before products reach the public [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who buys food, drugs, or cosmetics

how_it_helps.text: If the Secretary finds a reasonable probability that a food, drug, or cosmetic would cause serious adverse health consequences or death, the bill requires an order to immediately cease distribution, and after an informal hearing the order can be amended to require a full recall with notice to affected individuals [S2] [S3].

Any U.S. district court could order a manufacturer, importer, distributor, or retailer to recall a product found to violate the law, filling a gap in current law where recalls were effectively voluntary [S2] [S3].

The FDA Commissioner would gain subpoena power over witnesses and documents in investigations, and the agency could fine individuals up to $250,000 and companies up to $1 million per act — up to $3 million in a single proceeding — for violations, false statements, bribes to officials, destroying evidence, or obstructing investigations [S2] [S3].

Inspection authority would extend to foods and cosmetics as fully as it already does for drugs, and import screening would tighten: articles violating the law could be refused admission, dangerous refused articles destroyed, and violators fined [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors of FDA-regulated products, who would bear recall costs, new recordkeeping and reporting duties, broader inspections, and civil fines that could reach $3 million per proceeding; some of that cost could be passed to consumers in prices [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: A mandatory stop-distribution order could take effect on a 'reasonable probability' finding with only an informal hearing within 10 days, so a company could have a product pulled from commerce before full factual review — the strongest good-faith objection from regulated firms [S3].

The bill imposes new paperwork on every manufacturer, importer, and distributor, including mandatory reports of any company-initiated recall within days, and extends recordkeeping duties to all regulated products, which small firms would feel most [S2] [S3].
Companies could face civil penalties up to $3 million in a single proceeding for violations, on top of recall and destruction costs for refused imports [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is broad: faster removal of products that could kill or seriously injure people, and real financial consequences for hiding problems or bribing inspectors. The compliance costs are real but are the ordinary price of product safety regulation; the 'reasonable probability' standard for immediate stop-distribution orders is the part most open to fair criticism as potentially sweeping in products on thin evidence. On balance the bill traded modest, industry-wide compliance costs for stronger protection against dangerous products.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in November 1991, sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, got one hearing in May 1992, and never came out of committee or reached a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Edward Kennedy, who chaired the Senate committee to which the bill was referred, introduced it on November 27, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1] [S5].

The committee held hearings on May 19, 1992, printed as S.Hrg. 102-1183, but never reported the bill to the Senate floor, and no further action occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors of food, drugs, cosmetics, and devices are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory recalls, broader inspections, subpoena power for the FDA, and fines up to $3 million per proceeding. Consumers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to show how parties lined up: the bill had no cosponsors and never reached the floor, though its sponsor was a Democratic committee chairman.

industries.note: The bill would subject drug makers to mandatory recall and stop-distribution orders, broader inspections, FDA subpoenas, and civil fines up to $3 million per proceeding. Its enforcement provisions also cover bribery of FDA officials and obstruction of investigations.

For the first time, inspections of food would extend to equipment, processes, quality-control records, and consumer complaint files, and unsafe food could be ordered off the market rather than recalled voluntarily. Importers of rejected food could face destruction of the goods and a 3x-invoice-value bond for repeat defaulters.

The bill extends to cosmetics and devices the recall, detention, seizure, and inspection authority previously applied unevenly, and brings steroids and steroid substitutes under FDA enforcement powers.

industries.industry: Importers and distributors of regulated products
industries.note: Refused imports could no longer be freely relabeled or exported but would have to be marked 'United States refused entry,' and dangerous refused articles would be destroyed. Distributors and importers would owe new recall reports and recordkeeping.
